q2: Based on the findings of Marks (1987), we conjecture the following: (1) Human performance in the brightness classification task should depend upon whether there is a match or a mismatch between the visual target brightness and auditory distractor loudness. That is to say, responses to a bright (dim) visual target should on average be faster and more accurate when the simultaneously presented auditory distractor is loud (soft) than when it is soft (loud).

[PREREG_0013, relevance_score=0.364] This hypothesis will be tested with two ANOVAs performed separately on the mean response time (RT) and response accuracy data from the brightness classification task. This crossmodal correspondence between brightness and loudness should be reflected in both of the ANOVAs as a statistically reliable interaction effect between the two nominal predictors "brightness" and "loudness".

(2) Performance in the lightness classification task should on the other hand be independent of the intensity pairing between the visual target and the distractor tone. We therefore expect no Lightness × Loudness interaction in the analysis of the lightness classification data.

[PREREG_0014, relevance_score=0.379] Testing this hypothesis will involve two separate ANOVAs to be performed on the mean RT and error rates from the lightness classification.

(3) As implied by hypotheses (1) and (2), joint ANOVAs conducted on the combined data from the lightness and brightness classification tasks should further reveal Mode × Visual Intensity × Auditory Intensity interaction effects for both the speed and accuracy of performance.

[PREREG_0015, relevance_score=0.305] That is, there should be a statistically reliable three-way interaction effect between the mode of visual appearance (brightness/lightness), the intensity of the visual signal and the loudness of the auditory distractor on both RT and accuracy of performance.

(4) A within-subjects t-test will be performed on RT and accuracy rates from matching vs mismatching trials types to confirm that the crossmodal correspondence interaction effects are in the expected direction (i.e., faster and more accurate performance on matching type trials).

[PREREG_0033, relevance_score=0.260] (4) Supplementary analyses might be performed by recoding the congruency mapping between visual and auditory stimuli in accordance with each participant's perceived similarity ratings provided during the end of the experiment.

(5) More elaborate stochastic modeling of the latent cognitive mechanisms behind the loudness-brightness crossmodal correspondence might also be conducted.

[PAPER_0029, relevance_score=0.387] Method

Participants

We recruited 30 participants (19 female, 24 right-handed) from the student pool at the University of Tübingen, with a Mageof 26.2 (age range: 18-68 years). They were fluent German speakers and reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing. All provided informed consent and received either an €8 monetary reward or mandatory course credit for their participation in a single 1-hr session.

[PAPER_0030, relevance_score=0.484] Our choice of undergraduate students as the study population in this research seemed justified given that we did not expect individuals in the general population to differ much with regard to the basic perceptual mechanisms under investigation. Stopping rule for data collection was determined through an a priori power analysis based on iterative Monte Carlo simulation. Simulated RT data was entered into confirmatory analysis of variance (ANOVA) models 10,000 times per incremental step sample size.

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.365] Apparatus and Stimuli

Stimulus presentation and response recording was controlled via a Esprimo P956/E90+ computer (Fujitsu Limited, Tokyo) running the Python library PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) on a 32-bit Windows 7 OS. Visual stimuli were presented on a 24.1-in. FlexScan EV2495 LCD monitor (EIZO Corporation, Hakusan) placed about 60 cm in front of the viewer.

[PAPER_0046, relevance_score=0.254] Data Analysis

First, responses faster than 200 ms (0.02%) or slower than 1,000 ms (2.0%) were excluded from all data analyses. Incorrect responses (5.9%) were also discarded from analyses of mean RTs. Furthermore, the data of three participants were discarded from all analyses because of mean ERs above 15%.2 Mean RTs and ERs computed based on the remaining data were entered into separate three-way repeated-measures ANOVAs (Visual Mode × Visual Intensity × Auditory Intensity).

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.256] We also followed up on these three-way ANOVAs with two-way ANOVAs for brightness and lightness classification separately (Visual Intensity × Auditory Intensity), and we directly contrasted mean RTs and ERs from matching and mismatching trial types using paired t tests. Finally, at the suggestion of a reviewer, our preregistered analysis plan was complemented by a linear mixed-effects (LME) model analyses of the data.

[PAPER_0083, relevance_score=0.255] Sequential Analyses

In conflict tasks, CEs are typically larger after congruent than after incongruent trials (e.g., Gratton et al., 1992; Kerns et al., 2004; Stürmer et al., 2002). This congruency sequence effect (CSE) is commonly attributed to up-regulated cognitive control after conflict detection in incongruent trials (Botvinick et al., 2001). Against this backdrop, we investigated whether task differences between brightness classification and lightness classification also modulate the CSE.
